questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how a consultant should choose between manual entry, FBDI, ADFdi, and REST APIs for a data load into Oracle Fusion, per this course?
options: Manual entry is never actually used in a real Oracle Fusion implementation, because FBDI, ADFdi, and REST APIs between them cover every situation a consultant could ever run into on the job.
FBDI should always be the default choice no matter how few rows are involved, since its two-stage interface-table design makes it the safest of the four methods in every situation.

The choice depends on row volume and how often the load happens, but an occasional ad-hoc batch a finance user maintains themselves is best handled with a REST API, since REST APIs are the most powerful of the four methods available.

The choice depends on row volume, how often the load runs, and who's doing the work, not preference — FBDI fits large one-time or scheduled bulk loads, ADFdi fits small interactive batches, and REST APIs fit continuous unattended feeds.
ADFdi should be used for every data load regardless of size, since its immediate validation feedback is always preferable to waiting on a scheduled process report later.
REST APIs exist specifically so a functional consultant can run a bulk load without needing any coding knowledge or developer involvement at all.
questions.explain: The decision always follows three questions: how many rows, how often, and who's doing the work. FBDI fits large one-time conversions and large scheduled batches; ADFdi fits smaller, interactive batches a power user maintains themselves; REST APIs fit continuous, unattended, system-to-system feeds usually built by a developer. None of the four tools is a universal default.
questions.distractorExplain: The option claiming an occasional ad-hoc batch a finance user maintains is best handled with a REST API is the closest wrong answer, because it gets the ownership and cadence backwards: that exact batch size and ownership is what the course assigns to ADFdi, not REST APIs. REST APIs are reserved for continuous, unattended, system-to-system feeds typically built by a developer — not something a business user runs occasionally by hand inside Excel.

questions.prompt: A consultant has just run 'Load Interface File for Import' successfully for a batch of supplier rows. Has anything changed yet in the live Oracle Fusion application?
options: No — the rows are now staged in an interface table, but no real supplier record exists until the product-specific import process runs.
Yes — the suppliers are already visible on the Manage Suppliers page.
Yes, but only the supplier names are visible; the other fields are still pending.
No — nothing has happened at all, including the file not actually reaching UCM yet.
questions.explain: Load Interface File for Import only moves rows from an uploaded ZIP into an interface table — a staging area. Nothing in the live application changes until the separate, product-specific import process reads those staged rows, validates them, and creates real records. Confusing this staging success with final success is exactly the beginner mistake this lesson warns about.

questions.prompt: A consultant uploads a ZIP file of supplier records into UCM but accidentally selects the account scoped to General Ledger journal imports instead of the account scoped to supplier/procurement imports. What happens when the supplier import process's 'Load Interface File for Import' is then submitted?
options: It reports an immediate error at upload time, rejecting the file because it was filed under the wrong account.
It runs but processes zero rows, because the supplier import process looks for files filed under the supplier account, not the journal account, and the mismatch isn't caught until this point.
It automatically detects the correct account and reroutes the file before loading it.
It loads the supplier rows into GL_INTERFACE instead, since that's the account it found the file filed under.
questions.explain: Uploading into the wrong account doesn't raise an error at upload time — the file sits exactly where you put it in UCM. The mismatch only becomes visible later, when 'Load Interface File for Import,' pointed at the supplier import process, looks in the supplier account, finds nothing there, and reports that it processed zero rows — a confusing, silent dead end rather than a clear error.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the FBDI pipeline, from template to completed import, in the correct order.
items: Download the FBDI template for the business object being loaded
Populate the template's data tabs with rows of data
Generate the CSV files using the template's built-in macro
Zip the generated CSV files into a single ZIP file
Upload the ZIP file to Universal Content Management (UCM)
Run Load Interface File for Import to stage the rows into interface tables
Run the product-specific import process to validate the rows and create real records
Review the process logs and reports to confirm what succeeded and what was rejected
questions.explain: Every FBDI load follows this same sequence regardless of module: download the template, fill it in, generate CSV, zip it, upload to UCM, stage it into an interface table with Load Interface File for Import, run the product-specific import process that actually validates and creates records, then review the results. Everything before the final import step only ever touches a staging area, never live data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the button used to convert a completed FBDI template's populated data tabs into CSV files lives on the template's ________ tab.
questions.explain: Every FBDI template's Instructions tab explains what the template is for and holds the macro-driven control — usually a button like 'Generate CSV File' — that converts the populated data tabs into the CSV files the import pipeline actually needs.

questions.prompt: Select every item below that is a genuine FBDI template mistake described in this course — one that can cause rows to be rejected or silently mismapped.
options: Inserting or deleting a column on the template's data tab
Leaving old sample or placeholder rows in place below your real data
Typing a lookup's human-friendly label (like 'US Dollars') instead of its code (like 'USD')
Saving the completed template in its native .xlsm macro-enabled format before generating CSVs
Entering line-level invoice data on the header tab instead of the line tab
Using the template's own macro to generate CSV files instead of Excel's manual Save As CSV option
questions.explain: Inserting/deleting columns breaks the column-to-interface-table mapping; leftover sample rows get exported as if they were real data; typing a label instead of a lookup code is the classic rejected-row cause; and entering data on the wrong tab produces a well-formed file that's still structurally wrong. Saving in the template's native .xlsm format is simply how the file is supposed to be kept before the macro runs — not a mistake. Using the template's own macro instead of Excel's manual Save As CSV is the recommended approach, since the macro guarantees the column order a manual export can't.

questions.prompt: Match each part of an FBDI template's structure to what it actually is.
right: Named after, and structured to match, one specific interface table
Show the expected format, but must be deleted before entering real data
Explains the template's purpose and holds the CSV-generation macro button
Literal column names of the interface table underneath — never to be inserted, deleted, or reordered
questions.explain: The Instructions tab explains the template and holds the CSV macro. A data tab is named after, and structured to match, one specific interface table. Row 1's column headers are literal interface-table column names, never to be rearranged. Sample or placeholder rows only show the expected format and must be deleted before real data goes in.

questions.prompt: A template field expects the currency code USD, but a user types 'US Dollars' instead. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The row loads into the interface table without complaint, then gets rejected later when the import process checks the value against valid lookup codes.
Excel automatically converts 'US Dollars' to USD before the CSV is generated.
The CSV-generation macro detects the invalid value and refuses to run.
The row is accepted everywhere, since Oracle matches lookup values by meaning, not by exact text.
questions.explain: A coded lookup field expects the exact code, not a human-friendly label. Typing 'US Dollars' instead of USD doesn't stop the file from uploading or staging — that only checks file structure — but it fails later when the product-specific import process checks the value against valid lookup codes, exactly the kind of mistake that accounts for most rejected FBDI rows.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the course's 25-supplier worked example, 23 suppliers imported successfully, so exactly ________ rows were rejected.
questions.explain: 25 total suppliers minus 23 successfully imported leaves exactly 2 rejected — one traced to a duplicate supplier number, the other to an invalid supplier type code typed as a label instead of the correct lookup code.

questions.prompt: A consultant runs this query against the supplier interface table immediately after 'Load Interface File for Import' finishes, before running the actual supplier import process. What is the consultant trying to confirm?
options: That the staged interface rows match expectations — for example, that there are exactly 25 rows, not 23 or 27, and that values weren't truncated or reformatted.
That the suppliers have already been created as real, active supplier records.
That the supplier import process has already validated each row's business rules.
That the ZIP file was successfully deleted from UCM after loading.
questions.explain: Querying the interface table directly, before the real import runs, is a cheap sanity check: are there as many rows as expected, and do values like supplier_num look like what was actually typed, not truncated or reformatted. It catches a loading problem before it ever reaches business-rule validation.

questions.prompt: Match each Scheduled Processes status to what it actually means.
right: The process is queued, not yet started
The process finished, though it can still have rejected rows inside its own report
The process is actively executing right now
The process completed, but something inside it deserves a closer look
The process itself failed to complete — a more serious problem than ordinary rejected rows
questions.explain: Pending means queued, Processing/Running means actively executing. Succeeded means the process itself finished, which does not guarantee every row inside it succeeded. Warning often signals exactly that: something inside a completed process deserves a closer look. Error means the process itself failed to complete, a different and usually more serious problem than ordinary rejected rows.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Scheduled Processes work area, per this course.
options: Some processes, like Load Interface File for Import, can spawn child processes that do the actual underlying work.
Scheduled Processes is used only for FBDI-related jobs, never for other reports or batch jobs.
A parent process can still show as 'running' while its real work is actually happening in a child process row.
Filtering by process name and submission date is the practical way to find your specific run in a busy environment.
Every process submission produces exactly one row, with no possibility of nested processes.
questions.explain: Load Interface File for Import and Import Journals are both documented as spawning child processes that do the real underlying work, which means a parent row can still read 'running' while the real action is in an expandable child row. Filtering by process name and date is the practical way to find a specific run. Scheduled Processes is a general-purpose work area used for far more than FBDI — reports and other batch jobs land there too.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about an import process's execution report versus its log file, per this course.
options: The execution report is usually the first place to look for the business outcome — rows read, succeeded, and rejected.
The log file is a technical, often verbose record of the process's internal steps.
A completely clean report, with zero rejected rows, is guaranteed proof that every row you intended to load actually arrived.
The log file becomes especially useful when the report alone doesn't explain something, or the process errored before producing a normal report.
Reports and logs always show identical information, just formatted differently.
questions.explain: The report is the first stop for a business-outcome read: rows read, succeeded, rejected, and why. The log is a more technical, verbose record, most useful when the report doesn't explain something or the process errored before producing one. A clean report is not, by itself, proof everything arrived — rows can be dropped earlier in the pipeline in a way that never shows up as a 'rejection' in the import report at all.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of running and reviewing an FBDI import in the correct order.
items: Upload the completed ZIP file to UCM through File Import and Export
Submit Load Interface File for Import to stage the rows into the interface table
Query the interface table directly to confirm the expected row count and values before importing
Submit the product-specific import process to validate the staged rows and create real records
Review the process's execution report for succeeded and rejected row counts
Query the interface table and its rejections structure directly for any rejection the report doesn't explain clearly enough
questions.explain: Upload comes first, then staging via Load Interface File for Import. A direct query of the interface table before the real import is a cheap sanity check. The product-specific import process then validates and creates records. Afterward, the execution report is the first read of what happened, and a direct query of the interface table and its rejections structure is the second stop when the report alone isn't specific enough.

questions.prompt: A batch of 50 journal lines is staged in GL_INTERFACE. Every account combination is valid and every other field is correctly formatted, but the batch's total debits are $100 more than its total credits. What happens when Import Journals runs?
options: The entire batch is rejected, because General Ledger enforces debits-equal-credits across the whole batch, with no exception.
The batch imports successfully, and Oracle automatically posts the $100 difference to a suspense account.
Only the specific line causing the imbalance is rejected; the rest of the batch posts normally.
The batch imports successfully, since every individual line's account combination and format were valid.
questions.explain: Debits-equal-credits is checked across the whole journal batch, not line by line. A batch where every individual line is otherwise perfectly valid is still rejected as a group if its debits and credits don't net to zero — a validation rule that lives above the level of any single row.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Journal Import stages rows into ________, the General Ledger's staging table.
questions.explain: GL_INTERFACE is the interface table a Journal Import template's data tab maps to, holding account combinations, debit/credit amounts, currency, effective date, and journal category/source until Import Journals validates and posts them.

questions.prompt: An invoice header is staged with an invoice amount of $5,000.00, but its two line rows sum to only $4,950.00. The file uploads and stages without any complaint. What happens next?
options: Import Payables Invoices rejects the invoice when it checks that the line amounts sum to the header total.
Load Interface File for Import catches the $50 discrepancy and refuses to stage the file.
The invoice imports successfully with the header amount silently adjusted to $4,950.00.
The invoice imports successfully, and the $50 difference is written off automatically.
questions.explain: Load-time staging only checks that the file is structurally valid CSV, with no concept of whether a header total matches its lines. Import Payables Invoices is where that business rule actually gets checked, and a header/line mismatch like this one is exactly the kind of rejection that surfaces only at that later stage.

questions.prompt: Match each Financials module to the interface table and import process it uses.
right: FA_MASS_ADDITIONS, processed by Mass Additions Create, then posted in a separate step
AP_INVOICES_INTERFACE and AP_INVOICE_LINES_INTERFACE, processed by Import Payables Invoices
RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL, processed by AutoInvoice using grouping rules
CE_STATEMENT_HEADERS_INT, loaded from an external bank file such as BAI2
questions.explain: Journals stage into GL_INTERFACE for Import Journals. Payables invoices stage into their two header/line interface tables for Import Payables Invoices. Receivables lines stage into RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL, assembled by AutoInvoice's grouping rules. Fixed Assets candidates stage into FA_MASS_ADDITIONS, processed by Mass Additions Create and then posted separately. Bank statements stage into the Cash Management statement interface, usually from an external BAI2 file.

questions.prompt: Two receivables lines from a subscription billing system are meant to combine onto a single customer invoice through AutoInvoice's grouping rules, but one line's transaction date is formatted inconsistently with its sibling line. What is the most likely result?
options: AutoInvoice's grouping logic can't confidently match the two lines together, so the mismatched line is rejected or grouped incorrectly rather than silently combined.
AutoInvoice ignores the date-formatting difference and groups the lines together anyway, since grouping rules only look at the customer field.
The load-time file check catches the inconsistent date format before the rows ever reach RA_INTERFACE_LINES_ALL.
AutoInvoice automatically reformats the inconsistent date to match its sibling line.
questions.explain: Grouping rules assemble individual lines into transactions based on shared attributes like customer, date, and currency, before ordinary per-field validation even applies cleanly. A line missing a consistent grouping attribute can't be matched confidently, so it's rejected or grouped incorrectly rather than silently combined — exactly why reviewing AutoInvoice's rejection detail is part of normal Receivables troubleshooting.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the Fixed Assets create-then-post pattern in the correct order.
items: A candidate asset lands in FA_MASS_ADDITIONS, either from the Mass Additions Create FBDI template or automatically from a capital-coded Payables invoice line
Mass Additions Create processes the staged row into a formal, reviewable asset record
A reviewer confirms the asset category, useful life, and depreciation method are correct
A separate posting step adds the asset to the books and starts depreciation
questions.explain: Fixed Assets additions arrive in FA_MASS_ADDITIONS from either source, get turned into a formal record by Mass Additions Create, are reviewed by a person before being treated as finished, and only then get posted — a deliberate extra step beyond what journals or invoices require, since a mass addition often benefits from human review before it starts depreciating.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes FBDI's load-time validation from its import-time validation, per this course?
options: Both validation layers check exactly the same things, just at two different times, so a file that passes one layer always passes the other layer too.
There is really only one validation layer in FBDI; 'load-time' and 'import-time' are just two different names for the same single process.
Load-time validation checks business rules like supplier existence and account-combination validity; import-time validation only checks that the uploaded file is structurally valid CSV data.

Load-time validation only checks that the file is structurally valid CSV data; import-time validation is where real business rules — supplier existence, account combinations, debits equaling credits — are actually checked.
Import-time validation only runs at all if load-time validation already found at least one error somewhere in the file.
Load-time validation is an optional step that can be safely skipped whenever a file looks clean at a glance.
questions.explain: FBDI validates in two separate layers: load-time (Load Interface File for Import) only checks that the file is structurally valid CSV, with no concept of business meaning; import-time (the product-specific import process) is where real business rules — supplier existence, account combinations, line/header totals, debits equaling credits — actually get checked. A file can pass load-time cleanly and still generate dozens of import-time rejections.
questions.distractorExplain: The option that swaps which layer does what — claiming load-time checks business rules while import-time only checks file structure — is the closest wrong answer, because it gets both definitions exactly backwards. It's import-time validation that checks supplier existence, account combinations, and balancing; load-time validation never looks past whether the file is well-formed CSV.

questions.prompt: A 1,000-row FBDI payables invoice file imports with 998 successes and 2 rejections. A consultant fixes the 2 bad rows, then resubmits the entire original 1,000-row file again through the whole pipeline 'to be safe.' What is the most likely result?
options: The 998 already-successful rows risk being treated as new submissions, which the import process's own validation (like a duplicate invoice number check) will usually catch and reject, creating confusing interface-table logs along the way.
Nothing changes, since Oracle Fusion automatically recognizes and skips rows that already imported successfully.
The 998 successful rows are cleanly updated with any changes, and the 2 corrected rows import normally.
The whole batch is rejected outright, because FBDI never allows the same file to be submitted twice.
questions.explain: A row that already successfully imported is already a live application record. Resubmitting the same source row doesn't update it — it attempts to create a second one, which validation usually catches and rejects, but not always cleanly, and not without adding confusion to the interface-table logs. The safer pattern is always to isolate and resubmit only the rows that actually failed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about purging FBDI interface data, per this course.
options: Purging only successfully processed records is usually the routine, low-risk option to run regularly.
Purging all matching records, including rejected and never-attempted rows, is a more aggressive option that typically needs scoping parameters to avoid sweeping up unrelated data.
Purging a batch of rejected rows before reviewing and correcting them destroys the evidence needed to fix the problem.
Purging should always happen immediately after Load Interface File for Import, before the product-specific import process even runs.
There is only one purge option in Oracle Fusion, and it always removes every row regardless of status.
questions.explain: Purging successfully processed rows only is the routine, low-risk option. Purging everything matching a batch, including rejected and unattempted rows, is more aggressive and typically needs scoping parameters. The real danger is purging rejected rows before reading and acting on their error detail — that destroys the evidence needed to fix them. Purging is cleanup done after a batch is fully resolved, never right after staging and before the real import has even run.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the fix-and-resubmit workflow for rejected FBDI rows in the correct order.
items: Identify exactly which rows were rejected and why, using the execution report and interface-table queries
Correct only the specific values on those rejected rows, using a tool like Correct Import Errors or a small corrected file
Resubmit just the corrected set through the appropriate import process
Review the new execution report to confirm those rows now succeeded and no new rejections appeared
questions.explain: The workflow always starts by identifying exactly which rows failed and why, then correcting only those specific values, resubmitting only that narrow corrected set, and finally confirming the fix actually worked by reviewing the new report — never re-running the whole original file, which risks duplicating the rows that already succeeded.

questions.prompt: In the course's 200-invoice troubleshooting scenario, 187 invoices succeeded and 13 were rejected: 9 for an invalid supplier site (a trailing-space typo) and 4 for a line-total-versus-header mismatch. After both groups of corrected rows are resubmitted and confirmed successful, what should the consultant do next with the batch's interface data?
options: Purge the batch's successfully processed interface rows, now that the fix has been confirmed.
Purge all 200 rows immediately, including the original rejected ones, before confirming the resubmission worked.
Leave all interface table rows in place indefinitely, since purging is never necessary.
Purge only the rejected rows, but leave the 187 originally successful rows staged forever.
questions.explain: The scenario's final step is purging only once the new execution report confirms all 13 corrected rows now succeed with zero new rejections. Purging the batch's successfully processed rows at that point is the safe, routine cleanup — purging earlier, before confirming the fix worked, would risk destroying evidence still needed.

questions.prompt: A user clicks 'Create Journal in Spreadsheet,' but no ribbon or add-in controls appear in the downloaded workbook, and nothing happens when they try to use it. Based on this course, what is the most likely cause?
options: An ADFdi setup problem — the Excel add-in isn't installed or current, macros are disabled, or the add-in is blocked by security settings.
A journal batch that doesn't balance, which is being silently rejected before it reaches the spreadsheet.
An invalid account combination in the chart of accounts.
The interface table for journals is full and needs to be purged first.
questions.explain: A missing ribbon or an action that does nothing is the telltale sign of the tool itself not working — an installation, macro, or security/trust problem — not a data problem. None of the data has even had a chance to matter yet, since the connection to Oracle Fusion hasn't been established.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Create Journal in Spreadsheet enforces the same rule as FBDI's Import Journals — that total debits must equal total credits for the ________ as a whole, not just for each individual line.
questions.explain: ADFdi doesn't relax any business rule General Ledger enforces through FBDI. Debits must still equal credits across the whole journal batch — only the mechanical path to that validation changes, from a scheduled process report to immediate, in-spreadsheet feedback.

questions.prompt: Correct Import Errors (used to fix rejected FBDI invoice rows) and Create Invoice in Spreadsheet (used to create brand-new invoices directly) feel similar to use, with the same kind of connected-spreadsheet experience. Why, per this course?
options: Both tools are built on the same underlying technology, ADFdi, even though one is aimed at correcting rejected FBDI rows and the other at creating new invoices with no FBDI involved at all.
Both tools are actually the exact same FBDI template, just opened from two different menus.
Both tools require a completed CSV file to be generated before they can be used.
Both tools are REST API integrations wrapped in an Excel interface.
questions.explain: Correct Import Errors and Create Invoice in Spreadsheet are both built on ADFdi, even though they're used for two different jobs — one for fixing rows that already failed an FBDI import, the other for creating brand-new invoices with no FBDI involved at all. ADFdi is a general capability Oracle Fusion applies wherever direct, validated Excel entry makes sense, not a single-purpose tool.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about ADFdi troubleshooting, per this course.
options: A missing ribbon, a grayed-out action, or an upload that does nothing are signs of an environment/setup problem, not a data problem.
Once the tool itself is working, ADFdi can still reject a row for the same business reasons FBDI does, like an unbalanced batch or an invalid account combination.
ADFdi surfaces business-rule rejections in a scheduled process report, reviewed later, the same way FBDI does.
The temptation to resubmit an entire spreadsheet after fixing just one rejected row is the same mistake warned against for FBDI, just in a faster, more tempting form.
If the ADFdi ribbon doesn't appear, the first thing to check is whether the journal batch balances.
questions.explain: A nonfunctioning ribbon or a dead upload button points to an environment/setup problem, checked first before anything about the data. Once the tool works, it can still reject rows for the same business reasons as FBDI. ADFdi surfaces those rejections immediately, inline in the spreadsheet — not in a later scheduled process report, which is what makes it tempting (and wrong) to resubmit the whole spreadsheet instead of just the failed rows. If the ribbon doesn't appear at all, the first check is the add-in/macro/security setup, not a data question like batch balancing.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the tool and reasoning this course's decision framework assigns to it.
left: A nightly file of thousands of invoices from a supplier portal
A controller's ten ad-hoc adjusting journal entries this afternoon
A legacy fixed-assets register being converted at go-live
A recurring daily bank statement feed from an external bank file
A handful of invoices that arrived by email this week
right: ADFdi — small, interactive batch with immediate feedback, no file to build
FBDI — large, one-time conversion through the staging pipeline
FBDI — large recurring scheduled batch from an external system
FBDI — always, since bank files originate outside Oracle on a predictable external cadence
ADFdi — a few records needing fast, interactive entry with no batch file
questions.explain: Volume, frequency, and who's doing the work decide every case: a nightly scheduled file of thousands is FBDI; a controller's small, immediate, ad-hoc entry is ADFdi; a one-time legacy conversion at go-live is FBDI; a recurring external bank feed is always FBDI; and a handful of emailed invoices needing fast turnaround is ADFdi — the same three questions from lesson 1, now applied across all five Chapter 4 modules.
